description: Pull facts from two tables at once: INNER JOIN keeps matches, LEFT JOIN keeps every left row, RIGHT JOIN keeps every right row.

screens.body:
Real databases split data across tables instead of repeating it. Alongside students, we now have an enrollments table: student_id, course, grade — which student took which course.

Morolake (id 1) has two enrollment rows: CPRG 304 and CPRG 307. Noah (id 6) has none. And student_id 7 has enrollments but no matching student row — keep an eye on that row, it matters.

code.snippet:
-- the enrollments table
-- student_id | course   | grade
--          1 | CPRG 304 | A
--          1 | CPRG 307 | B+
--          2 | CPRG 304 | B
--          3 | CPRG 304 | C
--          5 | CPRG 307 | A+
--          7 | CPRG 304 | A

screens.heading: Why two tables?
screens.keyPoint: Each table holds one kind of fact.

screens.body:
INNER JOIN glues rows together where the ids match: ON students.id = enrollments.student_id. Only matching pairs come back.

Rows with no partner are dropped: Noah (no enrollments) and student_id 7 (no student) both vanish. Five matching rows come back.

options: Only rows where both sides match
check.question: INNER JOIN returns…

code.snippet:
SELECT students.name, enrollments.course
FROM students
INNER JOIN enrollments
  ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
-- 5 rows: Morolake x2, Tega, Ama, Priya

screens.heading: INNER JOIN — matches only
screens.keyPoint: INNER JOIN drops everything without a partner.

screens.body:
LEFT JOIN keeps EVERY row from the left table (students), even without a match. Unmatched students get NULL (empty) for the enrollment columns.

So LEFT JOIN shows all six students: Liam and Noah appear with NULL for course and grade. The five matches look exactly like the INNER JOIN result.

options: All six students, NULLs where there's no enrollment
All enrollments, NULLs where there's no student
check.question: LEFT JOIN students with enrollments returns…

code.snippet:
SELECT students.name, enrollments.course
FROM students
LEFT JOIN enrollments
  ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
-- 7 rows: the 5 matches, plus Liam and
-- Noah with NULL course; Morolake appears twice

screens.heading: LEFT JOIN — keep every left row
screens.keyPoint: LEFT JOIN never loses a row from the left table.

screens.body:
RIGHT JOIN is the mirror: keep EVERY row from the right table (enrollments). Now student_id 7 shows up with NULL for the name — an enrollment whose student doesn't exist.

You'll use RIGHT JOIN rarely, but know what it means: all right-table rows survive, left side can be NULL.

options: All six enrollment rows, NULL name for student 7
check.question: RIGHT JOIN students with enrollments returns…

code.snippet:
SELECT students.name, enrollments.course
FROM students
RIGHT JOIN enrollments
  ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
-- 6 rows: the 5 matches, plus
-- student 7 with NULL name

screens.heading: RIGHT JOIN — keep every right row
screens.keyPoint: RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table.

screens.body:
ON is what connects the tables: ON students.id = enrollments.student_id says 'glue where these two columns are equal.' The ON clause decides the pairs; the JOIN type decides which pairs survive.

WHERE is different: it filters the already-joined rows. ON = how to connect, WHERE = which connected rows to keep.

options: It says how the tables connect
check.question: The ON clause does what?

code.snippet:
SELECT s.name, e.course
FROM students AS s
JOIN enrollments AS e
  ON s.id = e.student_id
WHERE e.grade = 'A';
-- ON connects, WHERE filters after

screens.heading: The ON clause
screens.keyPoint: ON connects the tables; WHERE filters after.

screens.body:
Table names get long, so SQL lets you alias them: FROM students AS s, then write s.name instead of students.name. AS is optional — FROM students s works too.

Aliases don't change anything; they just keep queries short and readable. Aliased column names work in the SELECT list and ON clause.

check.question: With FROM students AS s, how do you write the name column?

code.snippet:
SELECT s.name, e.course
FROM students AS s
JOIN enrollments AS e
  ON s.id = e.student_id;

screens.heading: Aliases keep it short
screens.keyPoint: AS gives a table a nickname for the query.

screens.body:
Quick decision guide: want only rows that exist on both sides? INNER JOIN. Want every left-table row no matter what? LEFT JOIN. Want every right-table row no matter what? RIGHT JOIN.

LEFT JOIN is the one you'll use most — 'show me all X, and their Y if they have any.' In the exercises you'll rebuild all three with find() and map().

check.question: 'Show every student, and their courses if any' is…

screens.heading: Which join when?
screens.keyPoint: Most days: INNER for matches, LEFT for 'all of X'.
